title: On the Suitability of Syndrome Decoding for Proof-of-Work under Quantum Adversaries: Design and Analysis
authors: Aleck Nash, Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo, and Henry Chimal-Dzul
abstract:
Proof-of-work (PoW) remains a fundamental mechanism for
achieving decentralized consensus, most commonly instantiated using
cryptographic hash functions. In such constructions, mining takes the
form of an unstructured search problem over a large input space, where
miners repeatedly evaluate candidate solutions until a valid one is found.
While this design has proven effective in practice, it admits a quadratic
quantum speedup via Grover’s algorithm, raising concerns about the
long-term security of hash-based mining. Motivated by this limitation,
we investigate the use of code-based cryptographic problems as an al-
ternative foundation for proof-of-work. In particular, we focus on the
syndrome decoding problem and examine its classical and quantum com-
plexity based on current state-of-the-art information-set decoding (ISD)
algorithms and their quantum variants, comparing the resulting quantum
advantage with that of hash-based and lattice-based constructions.
Building on this analysis, we propose a proof-of-work construction based
on the Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) with a structured profile
constraint, which enables controlled variation of solution density and
difficulty. Under the standard random-instance heuristic, we derive ex-
pressions for the expected number of solutions and the probability of
successful mining, providing a principled basis for parameter selection.

On the Suitability of Syndrome Decoding for
    Proof-of-Work under Quantum Adversaries:
                Design and Analysis

       Aleck Nash, Henry Chimal-Dzul, and Kim-Kwang Raymond Choo

        University of Texas at San Antonio, San Antonio Texas 78249, USA



       Abstract. Proof-of-work (PoW) remains a fundamental mechanism for
       achieving decentralized consensus, most commonly instantiated using
       cryptographic hash functions. In such constructions, mining takes the
       form of an unstructured search problem over a large input space, where
       miners repeatedly evaluate candidate solutions until a valid one is found.
       While this design has proven effective in practice, it admits a quadratic
       quantum speedup via Grover’s algorithm, raising concerns about the
       long-term security of hash-based mining. Motivated by this limitation,
       we investigate the use of code-based cryptographic problems as an al-
       ternative foundation for proof-of-work. In particular, we focus on the
       syndrome decoding problem and examine its classical and quantum com-
       plexity based on current state-of-the-art information-set decoding (ISD)
       algorithms and their quantum variants, comparing the resulting quantum
       advantage with that of hash-based and lattice-based constructions.
       Building on this analysis, we propose a proof-of-work construction based
       on the Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) with a structured profile
       constraint, which enables controlled variation of the admissible solution
       density and provides additional parameters that may be used for dif-
       ficulty calibration. Under the standard random-instance heuristic, we
       derive expressions for the expected number of valid solutions and the
       probability that a generated puzzle instance is satisfiable, providing a
       basis for studying parameter selection.


1    Introduction
Proof-of-Work (PoW) is among the most widely adopted consensus mechanisms
and remains a fundamental building block in decentralized systems, most notably
in blockchain protocols such as Bitcoin, Litecoin, Zcash, and Tidecoin. PoW
facilitates decentralized security by permitting network participants, referred
to as miners, to dedicate computational resources toward solving formidable
cryptographic puzzles, a process known as mining. The first miner to find a
valid solution earns the right to append a new block to the ledger, validate the
included transactions, and receive a block reward. A defining characteristic of
PoW is its computational asymmetry: while the mining process is intentionally
resource-intensive, the resulting solution must be efficiently verifiable by all other
network nodes, thereby securing the blockchain against Sybil attacks [13].
2         A. Nash

    Modern PoW constructions predominantly rely on cryptographic hash func-
tions. In these systems, miners execute a high volume of hash computations to
identify a candidate that meets a specific difficulty target. This process essen-
tially reduces to an unstructured search problem over a vast input space. While
effective in practice, these designs are inherently susceptible to quantum acceler-
ation. Specifically, Grover’s algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for unstruc-
tured searches, effectively halving the security margin of hash-based PoW from
2d to 2d/2 . As quantum computing capabilities advance, this reduction poses a
significant threat to the long-term equilibrium and security of hash-based mining
systems.
    Motivated by this impending threat, recent research has explored alternative
PoW constructions based on quantum-resistant structured problems. Notably,
lattice-based proposals have emerged aiming to mitigate the quantum advantage
by utilizing problems such as the Shortest Vector Problem and its variants. For
these structured lattice problems, the best-known quantum algorithms offer only
marginal improvements over their classical counterparts [5]. This suggests that
replacing unstructured search with structured hardness assumptions may provide
a viable pathway toward quantum-resilient proof-of-work.
    Code-based cryptography stands as one of the most established pillars of
post-quantum cryptography, leveraging the computational hardness of problems
originating from linear error-correcting codes. This paradigm was pioneered by
Robert McEliece with the McEliece cryptosystem [18], whose security rests upon
the intractability of the Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP). This problem is
known to be NP-complete [6], and its presumed average-case hardness under
random instances forms the basis of numerous code-based cryptographic con-
structions. However, its potential as a quantum-resistant framework for PoW
remains largely unexplored within the cryptographic community.
Our goal. In this paper, we leverage the properties of the Syndrome Decoding
Problem in Coding Theory to propose a novel code-based PoW consensus mech-
anism. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first proof-of-work construction
based on the Syndrome Decoding Problem where the search for a low-weight
syndrome solution is utilized as a verifiable and adjustable metric of computa-
tional effort. We also provide an analysis framework for systematically evaluating
the proposal and motivating further research into whether structured code-based
problems can provide a viable foundation for PoW.
Our contributions. We make the following contributions:

    – Comparative complexity analysis. In section 4, we review the best
      known classical and quantum attacks on the Syndrome Decoding Problem.
      Information-set decoding algorithms and their quantum counterparts are the
      best known solvers and represent the current state of the art. We quantify
      the resulting quantum advantage and compare it with that of hash-based
      proof-of-work and lattice-based constructions.
    – A novel Syndrome Decoding based PoW. In section 5, we introduce
      a variant of the Syndrome Decoding Problem which considers a structured
                                                     2. RELATED WORK              3

   profile constraint that controls the distribution of the support solution to this
   problem. We then propose a PoW construction based on this variant. We
   show that the construction is parameterizable and permits explicit control of
   the admissible solution density, while practical difficulty calibration depends
   on the best profile-aware decoding algorithms.
 – Heuristic analysis of solution density and success probability. In
   section 6, we derive expressions for the expected number of valid solutions
   to the proposed profile constraint Syndrome Decoding Problem. By using
   this information, we compute the probability that a given instance admits
   a solution, under the standard random-instance heuristic. This provides a
   principled method for selecting parameters and controlling mining difficulty.
 – Implications for decoding-based mining. In 6.5, we analyze how the
   imposed structure interacts with modern decoding algorithms, in particu-
   lar Information Set Decoding techniques, and discuss how it affects success
   probabilities and overall complexity.

    Our results indicate that the quantum advantage in PoW systems based
on structured problems depends critically on the underlying problem and the
complexity of the best-known solvers. Syndrome Decoding exhibits a different
classical-to-quantum complexity gap than both hash-based and lattice-based
PoW constructions, suggesting that code-based approaches provide an alter-
native point in the design space of PoW mechanisms.
    We consider this work as a first step toward a broader exploration of code-
based PoW mechanisms. In particular, further research is needed to understand
how decoding algorithms can be adapted to exploit structure, to evaluate con-
crete parameter choices, and to assess practical deployment considerations.


2   Related Work

To mitigate the impact that quantum computing, especially Grover’s algorithm,
has over hash-based PoW mechanisms, several works have proposed PoW con-
structions based on structured computational problems. For example, Equi-
hash [8] introduces a memory-hard PoW based on the generalized birthday
problem, aimed at improving resistance to specialized hardware. More recently,
lattice-based approaches have been proposed, where mining is based on solving
instances of the Shortest Vector Problem using lattice reduction algorithms [5].
Ding [10] proposes a PoW based on multivariate cryptography, where the secu-
rity relies on solving random systems of multivariate quadratic equations over a
finite field.
    The Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) has been extensively studied in
code-based cryptography as a canonical NP-hard problem. The best known
classical attack algorithms against SDP are based on Information-Set Decoding
(ISD), with significant improvements over time through works such as Becker–
Joux–May–Meurer [4] and May–Ozerov [17]. Quantum variants of these algo-
rithms have also been developed, most notably by Kachigar and Tillich [15],
4         A. Nash

providing a detailed understanding of the classical and quantum complexity
of decoding. However, this line of work focuses on cryptanalysis and does not
consider applications to PoW, which requires specialized analysis due to its
structural properties, particularly its tunable difficulty and probabilistic solu-
tion space.


3      Preliminaries
In this section we present the necessary definitions and preliminaries for our
construction and analysis.

3.1     Proof-of-Work (PoW)
PoW is a computational mechanism that requires a prover to perform a tun-
able amount of work in order to produce a publicly verifiable witness. The idea
originates in the pricing-via-processing framework of Dwork and Naor [11], and
independently by [2] who proposed a hash-based PoW. Later, PoW was adopted
as the core mining primitive in Bitcoin [20].
    Formally, a PoW scheme consists of three algorithms:

                             ΠPoW = (Gen, Solve, Verify),

which are defined as follows:

    – Gen(1κ , D, r) → Cr : on input the security parameter κ, a difficulty descriptor
      D, and a public seed r, outputs a challenge instance Cr .
    – Solve(C) → w: on input a challenge C, attempts to produce a witness w.
    – Verify(C, w) → {0, 1}: on input a challenge C and a candidate witness w,
      outputs 1 if w is a valid proof for C, and 0 otherwise.

3.2     Linear Codes
Let Fq be a finite field with q elements and n ≥ 1 be an integer. A linear code
C of length n and dimension k is a k-dimensional subspace of Fnq . Such a code
                                                                             (n−k)×n
can be described
                  as the kernel of a full rank parity-check matrix H ∈ Fq
as C = y ∈ Fnq : HyT = 0 . The (Hamming) weight of x ∈ Fnq is denoted as
wH (x) and defined as the number of nonzero entries of x. The minimum weight
of C is wH (C) = min{wH (c) : c ∈ C, c ̸= 0}.

integers. Given H ∈ Fq           of full rank, s ∈ Fn−k
                                                     q   , and a positive integer
t ≤ n, find an error vector e ∈ Fnq such that sH (e) = s and wH (e) ≤ t.

    The SDP can be trivially solved using Gaussian elimination if we do not
require the condition wH (e) ≤ t. However, the condition wH (e) ≤ t is non-
linear and turns the SDP into a combinatorial search problem, which has been
proven to be NP-complete for an arbitrary parity-check matrix H [6, 3]. Note
that given a solution e to the SDP, verifying it is simple as it only requires
to compute sH (e) = Het and verify that sH (e) = s, which can be efficiently
implemented.


4   Comparative Complexity Analysis

The SDP problem has been studied for more than 50 years, and despite the
significant amount of research developed around it, the best algorithms to solve
the SDP are exponential in the number of errors that must be corrected. All
these algorithms are called Information Set Decoding (ISD) algorithms and the
first of them was introduced by Prange [22]. They all take advantage of the fact
that there might exist a large set of column positions of H containing an infor-
mation set (i.e. a subset of coordinate positions in a codeword that completely
determines the original message) of the code that is error free.
    For an [n, k] linear code C over F2 , the cost of computing
                                                                 an error vector
e of weight t in all these algorithms is O 2α(k/n,t/n)n , where α(k/n, t/n) is
a constant that depends on the rate of the code k/n and the ratio t/n. All
the research efforts to improve ISD algorithms have focused on decreasing the
value of this constant. In [15], values for the constant α(k/n, t/n) for the most
relevant ISD algorithms. Among them, the May–Ozerov algorithm has the best
running time with complexity O(20.0966n ) [17]. While the May–Ozerov algorithm
is an asymptotic improvement, it is widely considered a “galactic algorithm”.
This means that while it is mathematically faster for large values of n, the
constant factors and the memory overhead are so massive that it only becomes
more efficient than simpler algorithms (like Stern’s or BJMM algorithms) for
astronomical code lengths. Although May-Ozerov becomes advantageous only for
sufficiently large parameters, it currently provides the best asymptotic exponent
and is therefore used for complexity-gap comparison.
    The idea of applying quantum algorithms to accelerate ISD decoding was
first proposed in [21]. The approach in [21] of incorporating Grover’s algorithm
into classical ISD algorithm did not provide a significant speedup over classical
algorithms. However, in [15] Grover’s algorithm is used to find an error-free in-
formation set in combination with other quantum algorithms developed in [7] to
provide a significant speedup of quantum ISD algorithms. The best running time

6    Success Probability and Solution Density

In this section, we analyze the expected number of valid solutions and derive a
heuristic expression for the probability that a generated instance is satisfiable.
This analysis is used to tune the puzzle difficulty and to compare the proposed
construction with the standard syndrome decoding problem.
    We model the parity-check matrix Hr and syndrome sr as pseudorandom
and approximately uniformly distributed instances of the syndrome decoding
problem. This modeling assumption is standard in code-based cryptography,
where security relies on the hardness of decoding random linear codes [1], [4],
[17], [15].
    Our success-probability analysis follows the standard random-instance heuris-
tic used in decoding complexity studies, in which candidate supports are assumed
to behave approximately independently, and the number of solutions is estimated
via expectation arguments [4], [15], [19].
    This approach is analogous to that used in proof-of-work constructions, where
the success probability per attempt determines the effective difficulty of the
puzzle [8], [13].

6.2     Probability That a Fixed Vector Satisfies the Syndrome
Let Hr ∈ {0, 1}(n−k)×n be a parity-check matrix generated pseudorandomly
from the seed r, and let sr ∈ {0, 1}n−k be the target syndrome. Under the
standard random-code heuristic, we model Hr as a uniformly random full-row-
rank binary matrix and sr as a uniformly random syndrome. For any fixed vector
x ∈ {0, 1}n , the value Hr xT is then distributed approximately uniformly over
{0, 1}n−k . Therefore,Pr[Hr xT = sTr ] ≈ 2−(n−k) . This modeling assumption is
standard in code-based cryptography, where security relies on the hardness of
decoding random linear codes [9], [14].

6.3     Expected Number of Valid Solutions
In a proof-of-work setting, different public seeds r define fresh puzzle instances.
Under the random-instance model, these generated instances are treated as in-
dependently distributed for the purpose of analyzing solution existence. This
modeling assumption concerns the distribution of puzzle instances; it does not es-
tablish independence of optimized solver running times or rule out cross-instance
amortization.

6.5     Implications for Puzzle Difficulty
Modern decoding algorithms are based on structured search techniques such as
Stern’s algorithm, MMT, BJMM, and May–Ozerov style information-set decod-
ing (ISD) algorithms [23, 17, 4, 16], together with list merging and nearest-
neighbor filtering techniques. These algorithms construct partial candidates and
combine them to obtain a full solution. The profile constraint restricts the ad-
missible support patterns, and therefore reduces the number of valid solutions

7    Concluding Remarks
In this work, we studied syndrome decoding as a foundation for proof-of-work
and analyzed its classical and quantum complexity using state-of-the-art de-
coding algorithms. Our results quantify the corresponding classical-to-quantum
gap and place code-based constructions alongside hash-based and lattice-based
approaches within a unified framework. Furthermore, we introduced a profile-
constrained variant of syndrome-decoding proof-of-work that enables structured
control over the solution space and supports principled parameter tuning via
solution density and success probability analysis. Taken together, these results
identify code-based proof-of-work as a structured alternative to hash-based min-
ing with a distinct quantum advantage profile, and provide a basis for further
investigation of structured hardness assumptions in proof-of-work design.

 Limitations. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides a first analysis of
syndrome-decoding-based proof-of-work under standard heuristic models. The
                                            7. CONCLUDING REMARKS               15

results are based on random-instance assumptions and approximate indepen-
dence heuristics commonly used in decoding complexity analyses. While these
assumptions are widely used in the literature, they do not constitute formal guar-
antees. Additionally, our proposed construction does not eliminate the quantum
advantage: existing quantum ISD algorithms still yield a non-negligible speedup.
Our contribution is to quantify this gap and to show that it differs from that
of unstructured search. Moreover, the effect of the profile constraint depends on
how decoding algorithms interact with structured solution spaces. Our analy-
sis captures the baseline setting in which this structure is not fully exploited.
However, the extent to which it can be leveraged algorithmically remains open.
Finally, our comparisons are asymptotic and based on exponent-level models,
and should be interpreted as comparative indicators rather than exact runtime
predictions.

Future work. Several directions remain open. In particular, it is important to un-
derstand how modern decoding algorithms can be adapted to exploit structured
constraints, to evaluate concrete parameter choices in practice, and to investigate
alternative constructions that further shape the solution space. Additionally, this
work focuses on the construction and decoding complexity of the underlying com-
putational puzzle. A complete deployment in Nakamoto-style consensus would
additionally require analysis of precomputation, possible cross-instance amor-
tization, parallel scaling, and the distribution of block-generation times. These
protocol-level questions are left for future work. These directions may lead to a
more refined understanding of quantum advantage in structured proof-of-work
systems.
